title: Champollion Cracks the Code
objective: After this level you can explain how Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs.
summary: Thomas Young read the sounds of Ptolemy’s name; in 1822 Champollion showed that hieroglyphs mix sound signs with signs for ideas.

cards.headline: In 1822, a scholar burst in on his brother, cried “I’ve got it!” and fainted.
cards.body: In French, he said “Je tiens mon affaire!” The scholar was Jean-François Champollion, and what he’d got was the key to hieroglyphs. But he wasn’t the first to get a foot in the door. An English scientist had already shown that some signs spelled the sounds of a name.

cards.headline: Thomas Young’s head start
cards.body: Thomas Young was an English physicist, also famous for his work on light, who began studying the Rosetta Stone in 1814. He showed that some hieroglyphs on the stone spelled out the sounds of a royal name: Ptolemy. He also made major advances in reading demotic. That was a real crack in the wall. Most of the wall was still standing.

cards.headline: Too many signs
cards.body: Champollion tried counting. The hieroglyphic text on the Rosetta Stone uses 1,419 signs, while the Greek version has only 486 words. If every sign were a whole idea, those numbers should be much closer. So many signs had to stand for sounds, mixed with others that stood for whole ideas or objects. Hieroglyphs weren’t picture riddles after all. They were writing down a spoken language.
cards.callout: 1,419 signs for 486 words: too many for pictures alone

mascot.line: Sometimes the breakthrough isn’t a flash of genius. It’s just counting carefully.

cards.headline: Not just foreign names
cards.body: Maybe sound signs were only a trick for foreign names like Ptolemy? Champollion knew Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian, which helped him hear the sounds behind the signs. With it he read the name of Ramesses, a native Egyptian king. Egyptians had been writing sounds all along. On 27 September 1822 he announced it in Paris, with Thomas Young in the audience. The door locked since 394 CE was open.

cards.headline: The code: cracked
learned: Thomas Young read the sounds of Ptolemy’s name
1,419 signs for 486 Greek words: many signs were sounds

questions.prompt: Whose early work on the Rosetta Stone did Champollion build on?

options.label: Horapollo’s
options.rationale: He treated the signs as symbols, which misled people.

options.label: Napoleon’s
options.rationale: His soldiers found the stone; he didn’t read it.

options.label: Ptolemy V’s
options.rationale: He’s the king the decree is about.

questions.explanation: Thomas Young had already shown that signs in the name Ptolemy stood for sounds.

questions.prompt: Why did 1,419 hieroglyphic signs against 486 Greek words matter to Champollion?

options.label: It proved the stone was a modern forgery
It meant the Greek text was missing lines
options.rationale: The difference comes from how hieroglyphs work.

options.label: Too many signs for whole words, so many were sounds
It showed the hieroglyphs said something different

questions.explanation: So many signs couldn’t each be an idea; the script had to mix sound signs with idea signs.

questions.prompt: Horapollo (Level 91) explained hieroglyphs as symbols and allegories. What did Champollion show instead?

options.label: They were a secret code used only by priests
options.rationale: They wrote an ordinary spoken language.

options.label: They mixed sound signs with signs for ideas
They were an early form of Greek
They were decoration with no meaning

questions.explanation: Champollion proved hieroglyphs were a mixed system, with many signs for sounds, overturning the old symbol theory.
